course.title: Data Structures & Algorithms
course.description: Learn the data structures and algorithms behind fast software: Big-O, arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, recursion, trees, hashing, graphs and sorting, ending with a mini search engine project.

lessons.title: Big-O Notation & Algorithm Thinking
lessons.body:
What is Big-O?

Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory use grows as the input size n grows. It ignores small constant factors and focuses on the growth pattern, so we can compare algorithms fairly.

Think in steps

  1. Count the basic operations as a function of n.
  2. Keep only the fastest-growing term.
  3. Drop constants: 3n + 5 becomes O(n).

Common orders, fastest to slowest: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n), O(n^2) quadratic, O(2^n) exponential.

Example: linear search vs binary search

Linear search checks each item once: worst case O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Binary search halves a sorted list each step: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

def linear_search(nums, target):
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[i] == target:
            return i
    return -1

def binary_search(nums, target):
    low, high = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid - 1
    return -1

print(linear_search([4, 2, 7, 1], 7))  # 2
print(binary_search([1, 2, 4, 7], 7))  # 3

Time complexity: linear search O(n) worst case; binary search O(log n) but only on sorted data. Space complexity: both O(1) extra space.

Key points

  • Big-O describes growth with input size n, not exact seconds.
  • Drop constants and lower-order terms: 3n + 5 is O(n).
  • Binary search is O(log n) but needs sorted input; linear search is O(n).
  • Always state best, average and worst case when they differ.
  • Time and space are separate: a faster algorithm can use more memory.

mcqs.q: What does O(1) mean?
options: Time grows in proportion to n
Time grows with the square of n
Time stays roughly the same no matter how big n is
mcqs.why: O(1) is constant time: the work does not grow with input size, e.g. reading nums[0].

mcqs.q: What is the worst-case time of linear search in a list of n items?
mcqs.why: In the worst case the target is last or absent, so all n items are checked.

mcqs.q: Binary search on a sorted list of n items takes:
mcqs.why: Each step halves the search range, so about log2(n) steps are needed.

mcqs.q: An algorithm with two nested loops over n items is usually:
mcqs.why: The inner loop runs n times for each of the n outer iterations: n x n = n^2.

mcqs.q: Which is fastest for very large n?
mcqs.why: O(n) grows linearly, slower than O(n log n), O(n^2) and O(2^n) for large n.

lessons.title: Arrays & Strings
lessons.body:
Arrays: neighbours in memory

An array (a Python list) stores items in contiguous slots, so the item at index i is found by arithmetic, not by searching. That is why indexing is instant, while inserting in the middle is slow: every later item must shift.

Steps to use an array well

  1. Use indexing and append when order does not need shifting.
  2. Avoid inserting or deleting in the middle of a large list.
  3. Use two pointers for sorted-array problems instead of nested loops.

Strings are immutable

Python strings cannot be changed in place. s[0] = 'x' raises an error. Build a new string instead, for example with ''.join(...).

nums = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(nums[2])        # 30, O(1) indexing
nums.append(50)       # amortised O(1)
nums.insert(1, 15)    # O(n): 20, 30, 40, 50 shift right
print(nums)           # [10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50]

def reverse_string(s):
    return s[::-1]

print(reverse_string("hello"))  # olleh

Time complexity: indexing O(1), append amortised O(1), insert/delete in the middle O(n), linear search O(n). Space complexity: O(n) to store n items.

Key points

  • Array indexing is O(1) because items sit in contiguous memory.
  • Append is amortised O(1); insert/delete in the middle is O(n) due to shifting.
  • Python strings are immutable: build a new string instead of editing in place.
  • Two-pointer scans on sorted arrays often beat nested loops.
  • A list of n items uses O(n) space.

lessons.title: Linked Lists
lessons.body:
What is a linked list?

A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. Unlike an array, nodes need not sit next to each other in memory, so inserting in the middle only rewires pointers instead of shifting items.

Steps to insert after a node

  1. Create the new node.
  2. Point the new node at the current node's next node.
  3. Point the current node at the new node.

Order matters: step 2 must come before step 3, or the rest of the list is lost.

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.next = None

class LinkedList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None

    def prepend(self, value):
        node = Node(value)
        node.next = self.head
        self.head = node

    def to_list(self):
        out, cur = [], self.head
        while cur is not None:
            out.append(cur.value)
            cur = cur.next
        return out

ll = LinkedList()
ll.prepend(3)
ll.prepend(2)
ll.prepend(1)
print(ll.to_list())  # [1, 2, 3]

Time complexity: insert/delete at the head O(1), insert/delete at a known node O(1), search by value O(n), access by index O(n). Space complexity: O(n) for n nodes plus one pointer per node.

Key points

  • Nodes store a value plus a next pointer; no shifting is needed to insert.
  • Insert at the head is O(1); finding a value is O(n) because there is no indexing.
  • When inserting, link the new node to its successor before rewiring the predecessor.
  • Linked lists trade fast insertion for slow random access, the opposite of arrays.
  • Always keep a reference to the next node before changing a pointer.

lessons.title: Stacks & Queues
lessons.body:
Stack: last in, first out

A stack is like a pile of plates: you push items on top and pop them off the top. The last item pushed is the first one popped (LIFO). Stacks power undo, back buttons, and function calls.

Queue: first in, first out

A queue is like a line at a shop: items join at the rear and leave from the front (FIFO). Queues power print jobs, task scheduling, and breadth-first search.

Use the right tool

A Python list works as a stack with append/pop, but for a queue use collections.deque: popping from the front of a list is O(n) because everything shifts, while deque.popleft() is O(1).

from collections import deque

stack = []
stack.append("a")
stack.append("b")
print(stack.pop())   # b, LIFO

queue = deque(["x", "y"])
queue.append("z")
print(queue.popleft())  # x, FIFO

def is_balanced(s):
    stack = []
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    for ch in s:
        if ch in "([{":
            stack.append(ch)
        elif ch in ")]}":
            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
                return False
    return not stack

print(is_balanced("([{}])"))  # True

Time complexity: stack push/pop/peek O(1); deque append/popleft O(1); list pop(0) O(n). Space complexity: O(n) for n stored items.

Key points

  • Stack is LIFO: push and pop both happen at the top, in O(1).
  • Queue is FIFO: enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front.
  • Use deque for queues; list.pop(0) is O(n) because items shift.
  • Stacks check balanced brackets and track function calls.
  • Peek reads the top/front without removing it.

mcqs.why: A stack only allows access at the top, so the most recently pushed item is popped first.

mcqs.q: Push and pop on a stack cost:
mcqs.why: Both touch only the top element, so they do not depend on the stack size.

mcqs.q: Which structure fits a print queue?
mcqs.why: Print jobs must be served in arrival order, which is exactly FIFO queue behaviour.

mcqs.q: Why use deque instead of a list for a queue?
options: list.pop(0) is O(n) but deque.popleft() is O(1)
mcqs.why: Removing from the front of a list shifts every remaining item; deque is built for O(1) ends.

mcqs.q: Popping from an empty stack is called:
mcqs.why: Underflow means trying to pop when there is nothing to pop; overflow is pushing past capacity.

lessons.title: Recursion & Divide and Conquer
lessons.body:
What is recursion?

Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function needs a base case that stops the calls, and a recursive step that moves towards it. Without a base case, calls pile up until the stack overflows.

Divide and conquer

Divide and conquer splits a problem into smaller sub-problems, solves them (often recursively), and combines the answers. Merge sort and binary search both work this way.

def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:  # base case
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)

print(factorial(5))  # 120

def binary_search_rec(nums, target, low, high):
    if low > high:
        return -1
    mid = (low + high) // 2
    if nums[mid] == target:
        return mid
    if nums[mid] < target:
        return binary_search_rec(nums, target, mid + 1, high)
    return binary_search_rec(nums, target, low, mid - 1)

print(binary_search_rec([1, 2, 4, 7], 7, 0, 3))  # 3

Time complexity: factorial O(n) time; recursive binary search O(log n) time; merge sort O(n log n). Space complexity: factorial uses O(n) stack frames; recursive binary search uses O(log n) stack frames.

Key points

  • Every recursive function needs a base case and a step that shrinks the problem.
  • Missing a base case causes infinite recursion and a stack overflow.
  • Divide and conquer: divide, solve the parts, combine the answers.
  • Recursion depth costs stack space: factorial(5) uses 5 frames.
  • Naive recursive Fibonacci is O(2^n); memoisation brings it to O(n).

video.title: Algorithms and Data Structures Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners

mcqs.q: What must every recursive function have?
mcqs.why: The base case stops the self-calls; without it recursion never ends.

mcqs.q: What happens without a base case?
options: It recurses until the stack overflows
mcqs.why: Each call adds a stack frame, so endless calls exhaust the call stack (RecursionError in Python).

mcqs.q: factorial(5) makes how many calls including the first?
mcqs.why: Calls are factorial(5), (4), (3), (2), (1): five calls, returning 5*4*3*2*1 = 120.

mcqs.q: Merge sort's time complexity is:
mcqs.why: It divides the list log n times and merges in O(n) work per level.

mcqs.q: Naive recursive Fibonacci fib(n) is:
mcqs.why: Each call spawns two more, so the call tree roughly doubles per level: exponential time.

lessons.title: Trees & Binary Search Trees
lessons.body:
What is a tree?

A tree is a hierarchy: one root, branches to children, leaves with no children. A binary tree gives each node at most two children, left and right. A binary search tree (BST) adds order: left subtree values are smaller than the node, right subtree values are larger.

Steps to search a BST

  1. Start at the root.
  2. If the target equals the node, you found it.
  3. If smaller, go left; if larger, go right.
  4. Repeat until found or you reach an empty spot.

An inorder traversal (left, node, right) of a BST visits values in sorted order.

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(root, value):
    if root is None:
        return TreeNode(value)
    if value < root.value:
        root.left = insert(root.left, value)
    elif value > root.value:
        root.right = insert(root.right, value)
    return root

def inorder(root):
    if root is None:
        return []
    return inorder(root.left) + [root.value] + inorder(root.right)

root = None
for v in [10, 5, 15, 3, 7]:
    root = insert(root, v)
print(inorder(root))  # [3, 5, 7, 10, 15]

Time complexity: BST search/insert/delete average O(log n) when balanced; worst case O(n) when skewed into a line. Traversal visits every node: O(n). Space complexity: O(n) for the nodes; recursion uses O(h) stack space where h is the height.

Key points

  • BST order: left < node < right, for every node.
  • Search, insert and delete average O(log n) in a balanced BST.
  • A skewed BST (sorted insertions) degrades to O(n), like a linked list.
  • Inorder traversal of a BST gives values in sorted order.
  • Tree height decides cost: balanced height is about log2(n).

mcqs.why: The BST rule is left < node < right, which is what makes search skip whole subtrees.

mcqs.q: Average search time in a balanced BST of n nodes is:
mcqs.why: Each comparison discards about half the remaining tree, like binary search.

mcqs.q: Worst-case BST search, when insertions were already sorted, is:
mcqs.why: Sorted insertions build a skewed chain, so search walks down n nodes like a linked list.

mcqs.q: Which traversal of a BST gives sorted order?
mcqs.why: Inorder visits left, node, right, and the BST ordering makes that ascending.

mcqs.q: The root of a tree is:

mcqs.why: The root is the single top node; every other node descends from it.

lessons.title: Hashing & Hash Tables
lessons.body:
What is hashing?

A hash function turns a key into a bucket index, so a hash table can jump straight to the right bucket instead of searching. Python dicts and sets are hash tables. A good hash function spreads keys evenly across buckets.

Collisions

Two keys can hash to the same bucket: a collision. Common fixes are chaining (each bucket holds a list of entries) and open addressing (probe for the next free bucket). When too many keys pile up, the table resizes and rehashes everything.

scores = {"ana": 92, "ben": 78}
scores["cid"] = 85
print(scores["ana"])  # 92, average O(1) lookup
print("ben" in scores)  # True

def count_words(words):
    counts = {}
    for w in words:
        counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
    return counts

print(count_words(["a", "b", "a", "c", "b", "a"]))
# {'a': 3, 'b': 2, 'c': 1}

Time complexity: dict lookup/insert/delete average O(1); worst case O(n) when many keys collide into one bucket. Space complexity: O(n) for n entries, plus spare bucket capacity.

Key points

  • A hash function maps a key to a bucket index for near-direct access.
  • Dict lookup, insert and delete average O(1), worst case O(n) under heavy collisions.
  • Collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing.
  • Load factor (entries / buckets) triggers resizing and rehashing.
  • Only hashable (immutable) keys work: strings, numbers and tuples, not lists.

mcqs.why: Hashing jumps to the bucket directly, so average lookup does not grow with n.

mcqs.why: A collision is two keys sharing a bucket; chaining or probing resolves it.

mcqs.q: Worst-case dict lookup, with many collisions, is:
mcqs.why: If all keys land in one bucket, lookup scans that whole chain.

mcqs.q: Which can be a dict key in Python?
mcqs.why: Dict keys must be hashable (immutable): strings, numbers and tuples qualify; lists, dicts and sets do not.

mcqs.q: What does the load factor measure?
mcqs.why: Load factor = entries / buckets; a high load factor triggers resizing and rehashing.

lessons.title: Graphs & BFS/DFS
lessons.body:
What is a graph?

A graph is nodes (vertices) joined by edges. Social networks, maps and the web are graphs. Edges can be directed (one-way) or undirected, and weighted (with a cost) or unweighted.

BFS: level by level

Breadth-first search uses a queue: visit a node, enqueue its unvisited neighbours, then move to the next in line. BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

DFS: go deep first

Depth-first search uses a stack or recursion: follow one path as far as it goes, backtrack, then try the next branch. DFS is handy for mazes, cycle detection and topological sorting.

from collections import deque

graph = {"A": ["B", "C"], "B": ["D"], "C": ["D"], "D": []}

def bfs(graph, start):
    visited, queue, order = set(), deque([start]), []
    visited.add(start)
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for nb in graph[node]:
            if nb not in visited:
                visited.add(nb)
                queue.append(nb)
    return order

def dfs(graph, start, visited=None):
    if visited is None:
        visited = set()
    visited.add(start)
    order = [start]
    for nb in graph[start]:
        if nb not in visited:
            order += dfs(graph, nb, visited)
    return order

print(bfs(graph, "A"))  # ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']
print(dfs(graph, "A"))  # ['A', 'B', 'D', 'C']

Time complexity: BFS and DFS both O(V + E) for V vertices and E edges: each vertex and edge is handled once. Space complexity: O(V) for the visited set plus the queue or recursion stack.

Key points

  • A graph is vertices joined by edges; edges may be directed and/or weighted.
  • BFS uses a queue, visits level by level, and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
  • DFS uses a stack/recursion, goes deep first, and suits mazes and cycle detection.
  • Both BFS and DFS cost O(V + E) time and O(V) space.
  • Always mark nodes visited when enqueuing/pushing, or cycles loop forever.

Mark it visited and enqueue it

mcqs.why: BFS processes nodes in the order discovered, which is exactly FIFO queue order.

mcqs.why: Each BFS level is one more edge from the start, so the first time a node is reached is via the fewest edges.

mcqs.why: Each vertex is dequeued once and each edge is examined once.

lessons.title: Sorting & Searching Algorithms
lessons.body:
Sorting: put things in order

Sorting arranges data so searching and reporting become fast. Bubble sort swaps neighbours until sorted: simple but O(n^2). Merge sort splits, sorts the halves and merges them: O(n log n) in all cases. Quick sort picks a pivot and partitions around it: O(n log n) on average, O(n^2) worst case when pivots are bad.

Searching: find it fast

Linear search checks every item: O(n). Binary search halves a sorted list: O(log n). Sorting first costs O(n log n), so only sort when you will search many times.

def bubble_sort(nums):
    arr = nums[:]
    for i in range(len(arr)):
        for j in range(len(arr) - 1 - i):
            if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]:
                arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]
    return arr

def merge_sort(nums):
    if len(nums) <= 1:
        return nums
    mid = len(nums) // 2
    left = merge_sort(nums[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(nums[mid:])
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            out.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j]); j += 1
    return out + left[i:] + right[j:]

print(bubble_sort([5, 2, 9, 1]))  # [1, 2, 5, 9]
print(merge_sort([5, 2, 9, 1]))   # [1, 2, 5, 9]

Time complexity: bubble sort O(n^2) worst/average, O(n) best when already sorted with an early exit; merge sort O(n log n) in all cases; quick sort O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst; binary search O(log n). Space complexity: merge sort O(n) extra space; bubble/quick sort (in-place) O(1) to O(log n) stack.

Key points

  • Bubble sort is O(n^2): simple to write, too slow for large data.
  • Merge sort is O(n log n) always, but needs O(n) extra space.
  • Quick sort averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n^2) with bad pivots.
  • Binary search needs sorted data and costs O(log n).
  • Python's built-in sorted() uses Timsort: O(n log n) worst case.

nodes.label: Largest value bubbled to the end

mcqs.why: Merge sort always divides log n levels deep and merges in O(n) per level.

mcqs.q: Quick sort's worst-case time is:
mcqs.why: With a bad pivot (e.g. already sorted input and first-element pivot), partitions are size 0 and n-1, giving n levels of O(n) work.

mcqs.q: Binary search requires the data to be:
mcqs.why: Binary search discards half the range by comparing with the middle; that only works if the data is ordered.

mcqs.q: Which sorting algorithm needs O(n) extra space?
mcqs.why: Merge sort builds merged copies of the halves, so it needs linear extra space.

mcqs.q: Bubble sort on an already-sorted list with an early-exit check is:
mcqs.why: One pass with no swaps proves the list is sorted, so it finishes in linear time.

lessons.title: Mini Project: Build a Mini Search Engine
lessons.body:
What you are building

A mini search engine over a small collection of documents. It tokenises each document, builds an inverted index (word -> list of document ids), and answers queries by looking up words in the index and ranking documents by how many query words they contain.

Steps

  1. Tokenise: lowercase text and split into words, stripping punctuation.
  2. Index: for each word, record which documents contain it (a dict of sets).
  3. Search: tokenise the query, look up each word, and count matches per document.
  4. Rank: return documents with the most matches first.

This project combines everything in the course: dicts (hashing, average O(1) lookup), sets, sorting for ranking, and Big-O thinking about why the index beats scanning every document for every query.

import re

def tokenize(text):
    return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())

def build_index(docs):
    index = {}
    for doc_id, text in enumerate(docs):
        for word in set(tokenize(text)):
            index.setdefault(word, set()).add(doc_id)
    return index

def search(index, docs, query):
    scores = {}
    for word in tokenize(query):
        for doc_id in index.get(word, set()):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0) + 1
    ranked = sorted(scores, key=lambda d: scores[d], reverse=True)
    return [(docs[d], scores[d]) for d in ranked]

docs = ["Python is great for data science",
        "Data structures make Python fast",
        "Cooking recipes for dinner"]
index = build_index(docs)
print(search(index, docs, "python data"))
# [('Python is great for data science', 2), ('Data structures make Python fast', 2)]

Time complexity: building the index is O(total words); a query is O(query words x matching documents) instead of scanning every document word by word. Ranking the matches costs O(m log m) for m matches. Space complexity: O(total unique words + document references) for the index.

Key points

  • An inverted index maps each word to the documents containing it.
  • Tokenise first: lowercase and strip punctuation so 'Python' and 'python' match.
  • Dict lookup is average O(1), so queries avoid scanning every document.
  • Rank by match count; break ties by document order.
  • The same idea, at huge scale, powers real search engines.

mcqs.q: What is an inverted index?
options: A list of documents in reverse order
A map from each word to the documents containing it
A sorted list of all words
mcqs.why: An inverted index flips the mapping: instead of document -> words, it stores word -> documents, so a query jumps straight to matches.

mcqs.q: Why tokenise and lowercase text before indexing?
options: To make the index smaller only
So 'Python' and 'python' are treated as the same word
mcqs.why: Lowercasing normalises case so a query for 'python' matches 'Python' in a document.

mcqs.q: Searching with an inverted index is faster than scanning all documents because:
options: Dict lookup is average O(1) per query word
mcqs.why: Each query word is looked up directly in the dict instead of reading every document word by word.

mcqs.q: How should search results be ranked in this project?
options: By number of query words matched, most first
mcqs.why: A document matching more query words is more relevant, so matches are sorted by score descending.

mcqs.q: Which course data structure is the core of the inverted index?
mcqs.why: The index is a dict from word to a set of document ids, relying on average O(1) hash lookup.
